summary: Defines the Assured Forwarding group of Differentiated Services behaviors. It offers several traffic classes, each with different levels of how likely a packet is to be dropped when a router is congested. It lets operators give some traffic better odds of delivery than other traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: Assured Forwarding gives packets separate classes and levels that guide which packets a router drops during congestion. It aims to give packets within a traffic profile a better chance of delivery.

subtitle: Four forwarding classes with three drop-precedence levels for handling traffic during congestion.

tldr.problem: Networks need a way to give some IP packets a higher chance of delivery than others when traffic exceeds a subscribed profile or a router is congested.
tldr.mechanism: The Assured Forwarding group defines four independently forwarded classes, each with three drop-precedence levels. A congested node should discard higher-precedence packets with at least as much probability as lower-precedence packets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2597 defines the forwarding behavior and twelve recommended codepoints, while leaving specific algorithms to implementations. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 3260.

today: RFC 2597 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 3260. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Assured Forwarding Purpose
sections.content:
Assured Forwarding (AF) is a group of Differentiated Services per-hop behaviors. A provider can use it to offer different forwarding assurances for IP packets received from a customer network. The RFC's example is traffic that gets a higher delivery probability while it stays within a subscribed rate, with excess traffic receiving a lower probability.

AF defines four classes. Each class receives forwarding resources such as buffer space and bandwidth, and its packets can have one of three drop-precedence values. During congestion, a node tries to protect packets with lower drop precedence by discarding packets with higher drop precedence first. AF does not require a node to provide a particular delay.
sections.plainLanguage: AF lets a network give different traffic classes different forwarding resources. Within each class, a packet's drop-precedence value helps determine its chance of being discarded during congestion.

sections.title: Classes and Drop Precedence
sections.content:
An AF codepoint names a class and drop-precedence level, as in AFij. For general use, the RFC defines four classes and three levels in each class. A node should implement all four general-use classes, and it must forward each class independently rather than combine classes.

A node must allocate a configurable minimum of buffer space and bandwidth to each class it implements. It must accept all three drop-precedence codepoints and provide at least two different loss probabilities. Within a class, a packet with a higher drop precedence must not receive a better chance of forwarding than one with lower drop precedence. Packets from the same microflow in the same class must not be reordered.
sections.plainLanguage: AF has four separate classes and three drop-precedence levels in each class. A router keeps classes separate and must not give higher-precedence packets a better forwarding chance.

sections.title: Conditioning, Queues and Discarding
sections.content:
At a network boundary, a domain may shape or discard AF traffic, change its drop precedence or move it to another class. These actions must not reorder packets from the same microflow. If AF packets are tunneled, the tunnel's forwarding behavior must not reduce their assurance or reorder that microflow.

Within each class, an AF implementation must try to limit long-term congestion while allowing short bursts to wait in a queue. It must use active queue management, but the RFC does not require one particular algorithm. Its dropping behavior must react gradually to congestion and treat packets at the same class and precedence level alike, regardless of short-term burst patterns.

Random Early Drop is one example. In that example, discard probability rises between two congestion thresholds and reaches 100% above the second threshold. The RFC permits a range of behaviors and notes that this can produce inconsistent service between implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers should absorb short bursts by queueing packets and respond to lasting congestion by dropping packets gradually. The RFC sets required properties for this behavior but does not mandate a specific algorithm.

sections.title: Recommended AF Codepoints
sections.content:
The RFC recommends twelve codepoints for the four general-use classes. The first number in a name identifies the class, and the second identifies the drop-precedence level: 1 is low, 2 is medium and 3 is high. For example, AF11 is class 1 with low drop precedence, while AF13 is class 1 with high drop precedence.

The values occupy Pool 1 of the Differentiated Services code space. The RFC states that these recommended values do not overlap with other general-use per-hop behavior groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The AF name identifies both the class and the drop-precedence level. The RFC recommends a distinct codepoint for each of the twelve class-and-level combinations.

sections.title: Working Alongside Other Behaviors
sections.content:
AF codepoints can coexist with the local-use and Class Selector codepoints described in RFC 2474. The default codepoint 000000 may remain in use for best-effort traffic, and 11x000 may remain for network-control traffic.

An AF implementation should document which other behavior groups may use resources allocated to AF classes and how excess resources are shared. Preemption of AF resources must not happen during normal operation, though the RFC gives unexpectedly high network-control traffic as a possible exceptional case.
sections.plainLanguage: AF codepoints can coexist with other traffic behaviors. Implementations should document how those behaviors share resources with AF classes.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
A provider domain should limit incoming traffic to subscribed profiles to help protect against denial-of-service attacks. It should let the customer domain specify how link resources are allocated to AF packets. If an AF service depends on packet attributes such as source or destination address, the ingress node is responsible for checking them.

The RFC refers readers to RFC 2475 and RFC 2474 for other security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider should check that traffic stays within agreed profiles and verify packet attributes used to qualify for AF treatment. These steps help limit abuse of the service.
